notes.b: Burning is the everyday reaction that powers fires, cookers and engines. Chemists define it precisely, and then measure how much heat it gives out per mole of fuel, a quantity called the heat of combustion.
points: Combustion is the reaction of a substance with oxygen, giving out heat (and usually light). It is always exothermic, which means it releases energy to the surroundings, so the temperature around it rises.

Complete combustion happens in plenty of oxygen: all the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen becomes water. For hydrocarbons (compounds of only carbon and hydrogen) and alcohols the only products are CO₂ and H₂O.

Incomplete combustion happens in limited oxygen. It also gives carbon monoxide (a toxic gas) and soot (carbon), and releases less energy because less of the fuel is fully oxidised, e.g. 2CH₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO(g) + 4H₂O(l).

Standard heat of combustion, ΔHc°: the enthalpy change (the heat change at constant pressure) when one mole of a substance is completely burned in excess oxygen under standard conditions (25 °C, 101.3 kPa). It is always negative, because combustion is exothermic.

Because it is per mole of the substance burned, the equation for a heat of combustion has 1 mol of fuel, so fractions of O₂ may be needed, e.g. C₂H₆(g) + 3½O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), ΔHc = −1560 kJ mol⁻¹.
The same equation doubled, 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O, has ΔH = −3120 kJ, because twice as many moles of fuel burn and so twice as much heat is released.
notes.tip: If asked whether combustion is exothermic or endothermic, say exothermic and give the reason: it releases heat. When defining heat of combustion, say one mole, completely burned, in excess oxygen. A heat of combustion refers to one mole of fuel, so if you double the equation, double ΔH.

notes.b: Every complete combustion equation can be balanced by the same five steps. The order matters: carbon first, hydrogen second, and oxygen last, because oxygen appears in more than one product.
points: Step 1: write the formula of the fuel and the products CO₂ and H₂O.
Step 2: balance carbon. The number of CO₂ equals the number of C atoms in the fuel, since each CO₂ holds one carbon.
Step 3: balance hydrogen. The number of H₂O equals half the number of H atoms in the fuel, since each H₂O holds two hydrogens.

Step 4: balance oxygen last. Count the O atoms in the products, subtract any O already in the fuel (one for an alcohol), and divide by two for the number of O₂, since each O₂ molecule holds two O atoms.
Step 5: double everything if you want whole numbers, for example to remove a ½ in front of O₂.

Check: count each type of atom on both sides, and add state symbols (fuel, O₂(g), CO₂(g), H₂O(l) under standard conditions). The (l) for water is because standard heats of combustion are measured with water as a liquid.
notes.tip: Balance oxygen last, and remember the O atom already in an alcohol. Exams ask you to write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of a named hydrocarbon (methane, propane, butane) or alcohol.

notes.b: Each family of compounds follows a pattern, so one general equation covers every member. Here n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule. The range examined is hydrocarbons with no more than one double or triple bond, and primary alcohols (alcohols with the OH group on a carbon at the end of the chain) up to C6.
points: Alkanes (hydrocarbons with only single bonds): CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + ((3n + 1)/2) O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O.
Alkenes (one C=C, a carbon-carbon double bond): CₙH₂ₙ + (3n/2) O₂ → nCO₂ + nH₂O.
Alkynes (one C≡C, a carbon-carbon triple bond): CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ + ((3n − 1)/2) O₂ → nCO₂ + (n − 1)H₂O.
Primary alcohols: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH + (3n/2) O₂ → nCO₂ + (n + 1)H₂O.
notes.tip: Only primary alcohols up to C6 and hydrocarbons with at most one double or triple bond are on the course, so you never need to balance anything more complicated.

notes.b: These are the complete combustion equations for the alkanes, alkenes and alkyne you may be asked for, with water as a liquid. Where the fuel needs a half-molecule of oxygen, the doubled form gives whole numbers.
points: Methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
Propane: C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l), because 3 carbons give 3 CO₂ and 8 hydrogens give 4 H₂O.
Butane: C₄H₁₀(g) + 6½O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 5H₂O(l), or 2C₄H₁₀(g) + 13O₂(g) → 8CO₂(g) + 10H₂O(l).
Ethene: C₂H₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
Propene: C₃H₆(g) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).
Ethyne: C₂H₂(g) + 2½O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + H₂O(l), or 2C₂H₂(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l).
notes.tip: For a question like propene, you may give the doubled form, 2C₃H₆ + 9O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, to avoid a fraction. If you double the equation, remember that ΔH doubles too.

notes.b: Each alcohol already contains one oxygen atom in its OH group, so it needs less O₂ from the air than the alkane with the same number of carbons. Step 4 above (subtract the O in the fuel) is what gives these numbers.
points: Methanol: CH₃OH(l) + 1½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), or 2CH₃OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l).
Ethanol: C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), because the products hold 7 oxygen atoms, one of which comes from the ethanol, so 6 atoms (3 O₂) come from the air.
Propan-1-ol: C₃H₇OH(l) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l).
Butan-1-ol: C₄H₉OH(l) + 6O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 5H₂O(l).
Pentan-1-ol: C₅H₁₁OH(l) + 7½O₂(g) → 5CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l).
Hexan-1-ol: C₆H₁₃OH(l) + 9O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 7H₂O(l).
notes.tip: Remember the O atom in an alcohol when you balance oxygen. Alcohols give the same numbers of CO₂ and H₂O as the corresponding alkane; only the O₂ needed is different.

notes.b: These are the data values you are given and must be able to use to spot trends. Values are in kJ mol⁻¹ (kilojoules per mole) at 25 °C, with water as a liquid. All are negative because combustion is exothermic.
points: Alkanes: methane −890; ethane −1560; propane −2220; butane −2877. For example, each is more negative than the one before it.
Primary alcohols: methanol −726; ethanol −1367; propan-1-ol −2021; butan-1-ol −2676; pentan-1-ol −3331; hexan-1-ol −3984.
Two-carbon compounds: ethane −1560; ethene −1411; ethyne −1300; ethanol −1367.
Three-carbon compounds: propane −2220; propene −2058.
notes.tip: Give ΔHc a negative sign. Exams ask you to explain the trend in heats of combustion in a homologous series, and to compare alcohols with alkanes and alkenes with alkanes (Higher Level).

notes.b: In a homologous series (a family of compounds in which each member differs from the next by one CH₂ group), the heat of combustion changes in a very regular way. The reason lies in the bonds broken and formed for each extra CH₂.
points: ΔHc becomes more negative as the number of carbon atoms increases, by an almost constant amount for each extra CH₂, so more heat is released per mole of a longer molecule.
For alkanes the increase is about 650–670 kJ mol⁻¹, e.g. 1560 − 890 = 670 and 2877 − 2220 = 657.
For primary alcohols the increase is about 640–655 kJ mol⁻¹, e.g. 1367 − 726 = 641 and 2021 − 1367 = 654.
Each extra CH₂ group adds one C–C and two C–H bonds to break, and needs 1½ more O₂ molecules. It forms one more CO₂ (two C=O bonds) and one more H₂O (two O–H bonds).
More energy is released by the new bonds formed than is needed to break the extra bonds, so each extra CH₂ makes ΔHc more negative.
Because exactly the same extra bonds are broken and formed for every CH₂ added, the increase is nearly constant, so a graph of ΔHc against number of carbon atoms is a straight line.
notes.tip: When explaining the trend, state both parts: the increase is almost constant, and the reason is that the same extra bonds are broken and formed for every CH₂.

notes.h: Trend 1: estimating and predicting (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Bond enthalpies (the energy needed to break one mole of a given bond) let you put a number on the increase per CH₂. The regular straight-line trend also lets you predict a missing value.
points: Bond enthalpy estimate per CH₂, using C–C 348, C–H 412, O=O 498, C=O 799 and O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹: broken 348 + 2(412) + 1½(498) = 1919 kJ; formed 2(799) + 2(463) = 2524 kJ; difference −605 kJ.
This estimate is for gaseous water. The measured increase is larger because the water formed is liquid, which means extra heat is released when the vapour condenses.
The straight-line trend can be used to predict values, e.g. hexan-1-ol ≈ −3331 − 655 = −3986 kJ mol⁻¹, close to the data value of −3984 kJ mol⁻¹.
notes.tip: To predict a missing value, add the typical increase (about 654 for alcohols) to the previous member: for example, −2021 − 654 ≈ −2675 kJ mol⁻¹ for butan-1-ol, against the data value of −2676.

notes.h: Trend 2: alcohols compared with alkanes (Higher Level only)
notes.b: An alcohol and the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms give the same CO₂ and H₂O, yet the alcohol releases less heat. The difference comes from the oxygen already inside the alcohol.
points: A primary alcohol has a less negative ΔHc than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms, e.g. ethanol −1367 against ethane −1560 kJ mol⁻¹, and methanol −726 against methane −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
The alcohol molecule already contains an oxygen atom bonded to carbon and hydrogen (C–O–H), so it is already partly oxidised (it has already combined with some oxygen).
It therefore needs less oxygen (ethanol 3 O₂, ethane 3½ O₂), and less energy is released on complete oxidation, although the same numbers of CO₂ and H₂O are formed.
notes.tip: Say the alcohol is already partly oxidised, so it needs less O₂ and releases less energy. Don't say fewer C=O bonds form: the same numbers of CO₂ and H₂O are formed.

notes.h: Trend 3: alkenes and alkynes compared with alkanes (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Comparing compounds with the same number of carbon atoms but different numbers of hydrogens shows a second pattern. Fewer hydrogens means less water formed.
points: For the same number of carbon atoms, ΔHc becomes less negative in the order alkane, then alkene, then alkyne: ethane −1560, ethene −1411, ethyne −1300 kJ mol⁻¹.
The alkene has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane, and the alkyne four fewer, so fewer water molecules (fewer O–H bonds) are formed and less energy is released.
The main reason is the fewer O–H bonds formed, not the C=C bond being harder to break.
notes.tip: Don't explain the alkene trend only by saying the C=C bond needs more energy to break. The main reason is that fewer O–H bonds are formed.

notes.b: You can estimate a heat of combustion in the lab by burning an alcohol under a can of water and measuring how much the water warms up. This investigation uses primary alcohols to test how heat of combustion changes along a series.
points: Aim: to estimate the heats of combustion of a series of primary alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol) using spirit burners (small lamps that burn liquid alcohol from a wick), and to compare them with standard values.
Heat of combustion: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in excess oxygen.
Principle: the heat released by burning a measured mass of alcohol is absorbed by a known mass of water, so Q = m(water) × c × ΔT.
Here c is the specific heat capacity of water (the heat needed to warm a given mass by one degree) and ΔT is the temperature rise, so Q is the heat the water has gained.
ΔHc = −Q ÷ moles of alcohol burned. The negative sign is there because heat released by the burning alcohol means a negative enthalpy change.
Hypothesis (the prediction being tested): the heat of combustion becomes more negative by a roughly constant amount for each extra CH₂ in the alcohol.
notes.tip: Use the mass of water, not the mass of alcohol, in Q = mcΔT. Give ΔHc a negative sign.

notes.b: For a fair test, only one thing is changed, one thing is measured, and everything else is kept the same.
points: Independent variable (the one you change): the alcohol, i.e. the number of carbon atoms.
Dependent variable (the one you measure): the heat released per mole, calculated from the mass of alcohol burned and the temperature rise of the water.
Controlled (kept the same): the same volume (mass) of water, at the same starting temperature, so that the same heat gives the same temperature rise each time.
Controlled: the same copper can, the same distance from wick to can, and the same wick length, so that the share of heat reaching the can is similar for every alcohol.
Controlled: the same temperature rise (e.g. 20 °C), and the draught shield in the same position.

notes.b: The method is the same for every alcohol: heat a fixed mass of water with the burner, and find out from the change in the burner's mass how much alcohol was burned.
points: Step 1: measure 100 cm³ (100 g) of water with a graduated cylinder into a copper can (calorimeter, a container used to measure heat changes).
Step 2: clamp the can a fixed distance (about 2–3 cm) above the wick of the spirit burner, and surround both with a draught shield.
Step 3: weigh the spirit burner containing the alcohol, with its cap on, on a balance reading to 0.01 g.
Step 4: record the initial temperature of the water.
Step 5: light the burner and stir the water gently with the thermometer or a stirrer.
Step 6: when the temperature has risen by about 20 °C, put out the flame by replacing the cap, and record the highest temperature reached.
Step 7: reweigh the burner with its cap at once. The mass burned is the initial mass minus the final mass.
Step 8: repeat with each alcohol, using fresh water each time, and repeat each alcohol to check reproducibility (that you get similar results each time).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe a laboratory method of measuring the heat of combustion of a liquid such as methanol, including how to reduce heat losses and how to calculate the result.

notes.b: A labelled diagram earns credit in a description of this experiment, so know every part and where it sits.
points: Diagram: a copper can of water held by a clamp above a spirit burner, a thermometer and stirrer in the water, a draught shield around the burner and can, the burner on a heat-proof mat, and a balance for weighing the burner.

notes.h: Investigation: why each choice is made
notes.b: Every feature of the set-up either gets more of the heat into the water or keeps the measurement of the alcohol burned accurate.
points: Copper is a good conductor of heat, so heat passes quickly from the flame into the water.
The draught shield reduces heat lost by air currents and keeps the flame steady.

Capping the burner as soon as the flame is out, and weighing immediately, stops the volatile alcohol (one that evaporates easily) evaporating from the wick, which would otherwise be counted as burned.
Stirring spreads the heat evenly, so the thermometer reading represents all the water.
The same temperature rise and set-up for each alcohol make the heat losses similar, so the comparison between alcohols is fair even if the absolute values are low.
A temperature rise of about 20 °C is large enough to measure accurately, but not so large that heat losses, which increase as the water gets hotter, become very large.

notes.b: The calculation has two parts: the heat absorbed by the water, then that heat divided by the moles of alcohol burned. Here it is for ethanol, using sample data.
points: For each alcohol: 100 g (0.100 kg) of water heated through 20.0 °C gives Q = 0.100 × 4.18 × 20.0 = 8.36 kJ, using c(water) = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Ethanol (M = 46 g mol⁻¹, the molar mass): mass burned 0.63 g, so moles = 0.63 ÷ 46 = 0.0137 mol.
Heat per mole = 8.36 ÷ (0.63 ÷ 46) = 610 kJ mol⁻¹, so ΔHc(experimental) = −610 kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
Percentage error = (standard − experimental) ÷ standard × 100, e.g. ethanol (1367 − 610) ÷ 1367 × 100 = 55%.
notes.tip: Moles of alcohol = mass burned ÷ M, where mass burned = initial − final mass of the burner. Exams ask you to calculate ΔHc from the mass burned, mass of water and temperature rise, then compare it with the standard value.

notes.h: Investigation: sample results and graph (sample data)
notes.b: Repeating the calculation for all four alcohols gives a set of experimental values to compare with the standard ones.
points: Methanol (M = 32 g mol⁻¹): 0.82 g burned, giving ΔHc = −326 kJ mol⁻¹.
Propan-1-ol (M = 60 g mol⁻¹): 0.55 g burned, giving ΔHc = −912 kJ mol⁻¹.
Butan-1-ol (M = 74 g mol⁻¹): 0.51 g burned, giving ΔHc = −1210 kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.
Standard values are −726, −1367, −2021 and −2676 kJ mol⁻¹; each experimental value is about 45% of the standard value.
A graph of experimental ΔHc against number of carbon atoms is a straight line, like the standard values but less steep, so the trend is confirmed even though the values are too low.
notes.tip: Experimental values are less negative than standard values. A value more negative than the standard means an error in the data or calculation.

notes.b: The experimental values come out far below the standard ones. A good answer says why each error makes the value too low, not just that it is a problem.
points: Heat loss: much of the heat from the flame goes to the surrounding air rather than into the water; this is the main reason the values are much less negative than standard values.

Heat absorbed by the copper can, thermometer and clamp is not included in Q, so less heat is measured in the water and the value is too small. It could be added as m(copper) × c(copper) × ΔT, with c(copper) ≈ 0.385 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Incomplete combustion: with limited air at the wick, some carbon forms soot, seen on the base of the can, and carbon monoxide, releasing less energy than complete combustion.
Evaporation of alcohol from the wick: alcohol lost without burning is counted as burned, making the heat per mole too small.
Non-standard conditions: standard values assume products at 25 °C with water as a liquid; in the experiment the water leaves as vapour, so its heat of condensation is not released into the can.
Improvements to reduce heat loss: insulate the can and add a lid, reduce the distance between flame and can, and use a draught shield.
Improvements to reduce other errors: ensure a good air supply for complete combustion, cap and weigh the burner immediately, and include the heat absorbed by the can.
Accurate values are measured in a sealed calorimeter, which is not required here.
notes.tip: Sources of error must explain the direction of the difference (why the value is too low), not just list problems. Exams ask for the main sources of error.

notes.b: Alcohols burn easily and methanol is poisonous, so the main precautions are about fire and fumes.
points: Alcohols are highly flammable: keep bottles stoppered and away from flames, never refill a burner while it is lit or hot, and refill in a fume cupboard or away from flames.
Methanol is toxic by swallowing, by skin contact and by inhaling its vapour; avoid skin contact and work in a well-ventilated room.
Wear safety glasses, tie back long hair, stand the burner on a heat-proof mat, and let the copper can cool before handling it.

keyTerms.definition: The reaction of a substance with oxygen, giving out heat and usually light.
Burning in plenty of oxygen, so that all the carbon becomes CO₂ and all the hydrogen becomes H₂O.
Burning in limited oxygen, which forms carbon monoxide and soot and releases less energy.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in excess oxygen under standard conditions.
A family of compounds with the same general formula, in which each member differs from the next by one CH₂ group.
An alcohol in which the carbon bearing the –OH group is bonded to only one other carbon atom, such as ethanol.
A hydrocarbon containing only single C–C and C–H bonds.
A hydrocarbon containing one C=C double bond.
A hydrocarbon containing one C≡C triple bond.
The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in excess oxygen.
A small burner that holds liquid alcohol in a container with a wick, used to heat water in a heat-of-combustion experiment.
A container, such as a copper can, that holds water so that the heat released by burning can be measured.
A screen placed around the burner and can to reduce heat lost by air currents.
The factor that the experimenter deliberately changes, here the alcohol.
The factor that is measured in response to the change, here the heat released per mole.
A factor that is kept the same so that it does not affect the results.
The difference between the standard and experimental values, divided by the standard value and multiplied by 100.
Describes a liquid that evaporates easily at room temperature.

questions.prompt: Write balanced equations for the complete combustion of (i) propene, (ii) propan-1-ol, (iii) hexan-1-ol.
questions.model: (i) Propene: C₃H₆(g) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), or 2C₃H₆(g) + 9O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l). (ii) Propan-1-ol: C₃H₇OH(l) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l). (iii) Hexan-1-ol: C₆H₁₃OH(l) + 9O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 7H₂O(l). Each equation was balanced by balancing carbon, then hydrogen, then oxygen last, counting the O atom in the alcohol.

questions.prompt: The standard heats of combustion of methanol, ethanol and propan-1-ol are −726, −1367 and −2021 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain the trend and use it to predict the heat of combustion of butan-1-ol.
questions.model: Each extra CH₂ group makes ΔHc more negative by an almost constant amount, about 640–655 kJ mol⁻¹. The extra CH₂ adds one C–C and two C–H bonds to break, and one more CO₂ (two C=O bonds) and one more H₂O (two O–H bonds) form. More energy is released by the new bonds formed than is needed to break the extra bonds, so the value becomes more negative. Ethanol to propan-1-ol changes by −2021 − (−1367) = −654 kJ mol⁻¹. Predicted ΔHc of butan-1-ol = −2021 − 654 ≈ −2675 kJ mol⁻¹; the data value is −2676 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Explain why the heat of combustion of ethanol (−1367 kJ mol⁻¹) is less negative than that of ethane (−1560 kJ mol⁻¹), and why that of ethene (−1411 kJ mol⁻¹) is less negative than that of ethane.
questions.model: Ethanol is already partly oxidised, because its molecule contains a C–O–H group. It therefore needs less oxygen (3 mol O₂, against 3½ mol for ethane) and less energy is released on complete oxidation, although both form 2 mol CO₂ and 3 mol H₂O. Ethene has two fewer hydrogen atoms than ethane, so fewer water molecules, and fewer O–H bonds, are formed on combustion. Less energy is released, so its heat of combustion is less negative than that of ethane.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would estimate the heat of combustion of ethanol using a spirit burner, including how you would reduce heat losses and how you would calculate the result.
questions.model: Measure 100 cm³ (100 g) of water into a copper can and clamp the can about 2–3 cm above the wick of the spirit burner, inside a draught shield. Weigh the burner containing the ethanol, with its cap on, to 0.01 g. Record the initial temperature of the water. Light the burner, stir the water gently, and when the temperature has risen by about 20 °C, put out the flame by replacing the cap and record the highest temperature. Reweigh the burner with its cap at once, and repeat with fresh water. Heat losses are reduced by the copper can, which conducts heat well into the water, by the draught shield, which reduces heat lost by air currents, and by capping the burner and weighing it immediately, which stops ethanol evaporating from the wick. To calculate the result, use Q = m × c × ΔT with m = 0.100 kg, c = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ΔT = 20.0 K. Find the moles of ethanol burned from the mass lost and M = 46 g mol⁻¹. Then ΔHc = −Q ÷ moles of ethanol burned.

questions.prompt: Burning 0.70 g of ethanol raised the temperature of 150 g of water by 20.0 °C. Calculate the heat of combustion of ethanol (c = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; C₂H₅OH = 46), compare it with the standard value of −1367 kJ mol⁻¹, and account for the difference (sample data).
questions.model: Q = 0.150 kg × 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 20.0 K = 12.54 kJ. Moles of ethanol = 0.70 g ÷ 46 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0152 mol. ΔHc = −12.54 kJ ÷ 0.0152 mol = −824 kJ mol⁻¹. This is about 60% of the standard value of −1367 kJ mol⁻¹, so the experimental value is much less negative. The difference is mainly due to heat lost to the surrounding air, which does not reach the water. Incomplete combustion, forming soot and carbon monoxide, releases less energy. Some ethanol may evaporate from the wick without burning, which is counted as burned and makes the heat per mole too small. The standard value assumes water as a liquid, but in the experiment the water leaves as vapour, so its heat of condensation is not released into the can.

questions.prompt: A student measured the heats of combustion of four alcohols. Explain why the experimental values were all much less negative than the standard values, but still showed the same trend.
questions.model: Much of the heat from the flame is lost to the surrounding air rather than going into the water, and heat is absorbed by the copper can, thermometer and clamp, so the values are much less negative than the standard values. Incomplete combustion forming soot and carbon monoxide releases less energy, and alcohol evaporating from the wick is counted as burned, which makes the heat per mole too small. These errors are similar for each alcohol because the same apparatus and temperature rise are used for each, so the experimental values still fall by a roughly constant amount for each extra CH₂ group, and the trend is confirmed.
